item.title: The State That Remembers
item.dc:creator: Christopher A. Pissarides and Fadi Farra
item.description: Although many economists believe that AI could drive an economic transformation larger than the Industrial Revolution, and on a vastly shorter timetable, most governments are unequipped to manage such a transition. We urgently need states that can learn on the go and remember what they learn.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: mihailomilovanovic/Getty Images

Although many economists believe that AI could drive an economic transformation larger than the Industrial Revolution, and on a vastly shorter timetable, most governments are unequipped to manage such a transition. We urgently need states that can learn on the go and remember what they learn.

By Christopher A. Pissarides and Fadi Farra

LONDON—Just as companies refine what they know about their customers with every click, purchase, and failed transaction, government-provided services collect information about their clients, commission evaluations, and employ armies of analysts. Yet many governments cannot articulate what they believe about a given policy: what effect they expect it to produce, how confident they are, and which evidence would change their minds.

item.title: The End of Abundance
item.dc:creator: V. Anantha Nageswaran
item.description: The decades ahead will be shaped by a contest for natural resources, making the world more prone to stagflation and handing the levers of policy back to governments. Emerging economies that are rich in people but poor in resources will be the most acutely affected but can take practical steps to strengthen their resilience.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Rodger Bosch/AFP via Getty Images

The decades ahead will be shaped by a contest for natural resources, making the world more prone to stagflation and handing the levers of policy back to governments. Emerging economies that are rich in people but poor in resources will be the most acutely affected but can take practical steps to strengthen their resilience.

By V. Anantha Nageswaran

NEW DELHI—From the early 1980s until the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020, the world economy enjoyed unusually good conditions. The Cold War ended, defense budgets shrank, and hundreds of millions of workers joined the global market. Energy and metals were mostly cheap, and supply chains stretched across borders on the assumption that goods would always move freely. Inflation was on a downward trend, owing partly to central banks and partly to the strong tide of peace, globalization, and plentiful supply they were swimming in.

item.title: A Global Euro Must First Win Over Europe
item.dc:creator: Piroska Nagy Mohácsi
item.description: In a world of competing currency blocs, the euro is the dollar’s most credible rival. But for it to become a genuine counterweight to the greenback, the European Union must strengthen its financial foundations and expand its reach, starting with the member states that have not adopted it despite being obliged to do so.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images

In a world of competing currency blocs, the euro is the dollar’s most credible rival. But for it to become a genuine counterweight to the greenback, the European Union must strengthen its financial foundations and expand its reach, starting with the member states that have not adopted it despite being obliged to do so.

By Piroska Nagy Mohácsi

LONDON—As the global monetary order becomes increasingly fragmented, the European Union has a rare opportunity to shape the emerging system and bolster the euro’s international role. But for the euro to become genuinely global, it must first become more European.

item.title: Japan Needs Higher Interest Rates
item.dc:creator: Koichi Hamada
item.description: In 2012, when Japan was dealing with chronic deflation, policymakers were right to embrace monetary easing, including lower interest rates. Today, however, Japan faces the opposite problem: a weak yen, combined with higher interest rates in the US, calls for a much tighter monetary policy.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Richard A. Brooks/AFP via Getty Images

In 2012, when Japan was dealing with chronic deflation, policymakers were right to embrace monetary easing, including lower interest rates. Today, however, Japan faces the opposite problem: a weak yen, combined with higher interest rates in the US, calls for a much tighter monetary policy.

By Koichi Hamada

NEW HAVEN—On a recent visit to Sapporo, the city on Japan’s northern island where my parents came from, my wife and I found gentle people, mild autumn days, and excellent food. As tourists who live and work in the United States, we also enjoyed very low prices: lunch at a high-quality restaurant cost only about $20 per person. While that was convenient for us, like so many other tourists who have headed to Japan to take advantage of favorable exchange rates, the cheap yen (yen yasu) has been hard on Japan’s economy.

item.title: A Middle-Powers Grand Strategy to Prevent Atrocities
item.dc:creator: Aarif Abraham
item.description: Many governments have leverage to prevent atrocity crimes, yet lack the machinery to turn warnings into consistent, accountable action before it is too late. Now that three of the five permanent members of the Security Council are undercutting the postwar legal order, middle powers most close the gap.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Adam Pretty/Getty Images

Many governments have leverage to prevent atrocity crimes, yet lack the machinery to turn warnings into consistent, accountable action before it is too late. Now that three of the five permanent members of the Security Council are undercutting the postwar legal order, middle powers most close the gap.

By Aarif Abraham

LONDON—“Never again” to genocide is one of the international community’s most brittle postwar promises, often invoked only after the killing has begun. Yet mass atrocities seldom arrive without warning. Attacks on the rule of law, discrimination, dehumanization, and impunity for earlier crimes are familiar, easily discernible precursors.

item.title: Unleashing Africa’s Women Agripreneurs
item.dc:creator: Ana Maria Loboguerrero
item.description: Across Sub-Saharan Africa, women workers dominate agriculture but rarely capture the sector’s economic value. With a systematic approach to closing the gap, policymakers, NGOs, and philanthropic organizations could unlock a $1 trillion market and transform the continent’s food systems for the better.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Godong Universal Images Group/Getty Images

Across Sub-Saharan Africa, women workers dominate agriculture but rarely capture the sector’s economic value. With a systematic approach to closing the gap, policymakers, NGOs, and philanthropic organizations could unlock a $1 trillion market and transform the continent’s food systems for the better.

By Ana Maria Loboguerrero

WASHINGTON, DC—If you picture a woman working in agriculture in Africa, what image comes to mind? Maybe it’s a young woman with an infant slung on her back, hacking at the soil in searing heat, struggling to find affordable fertilizer or a decent price for her crop. Or maybe she’s a successful entrepreneur building a vibrant food business, employing hundreds of workers, and contributing much to her local economy.

Both women are real, of course, as are many variations in between. But the fact is that many more women could be leading farming businesses and driving economic growth if the barriers they face were tackled more systematically. With Africa’s food and agriculture market predicted to reach around $1 trillion by 2030, countries that want to harness the most value cannot afford to forgo women’s economic power.

In Sub-Saharan Africa, over three-quarters of working women can be found in the agrifood sector, where around two-thirds of their work happens off the farm, in processing, aggregation, storage, and informal trade. Although these are the links in the chain where value is added, the women performing such roles often remain trapped in precarious, low-paid, informal arrangements.

At the other end of the spectrum is a growing cadre of dynamic African women food entrepreneurs or “agripreneurs.” I recently encountered some of these women business leaders at the Africa Food Systems Forum in Rwanda, where they were being honored for their success.

Ifeoma Mary Okonkwo, for example, co-founded a solar-powered cassava business in Nigeria that processes 15 tons per day into gluten-free flour, starch, fortified foods, and animal feed for domestic and export markets. In the space of a decade, her company has grown to employ hundreds of people. It has purchased cassava worth more than $4.45 million from its network of 2,000 (mostly women) farmers, while helping them access fertilizer, technical advice, and markets.

Okonkwo’s story shows what can happen when governments and donors make a deliberate effort to empower women-led businesses. Among other advantages, she was able to access finance on favorable terms through women-focused lending schemes.

But much more must be done. A recent World Bank report, Women, Business, and the Law 2026, shows that legal equality on paper does not automatically produce economic opportunity. Women may have the right to register a business or open a line of credit, but their ability to formalize operations, invest, and expand is still limited by weak enforcement, a thin financial infrastructure, restrictive social norms, or unpaid care work.

Updating antiquated land ownership laws would be a good start, since inheritance customs and social norms routinely override women’s legal land rights in practice. Still, passing a law isn’t the same as enforcing it, and the same caveat applies to gender-equal business laws. In each case, implementing legal changes matters as much as enacting them.

Fortunately, when it comes to empowering rural women to move from subsistence farming to viable small businesses, a growing body of evidence shows what works. In Ethiopia, for example, agriculture employs around 80% of the country’s workforce, yet female farm managers were producing at least one-third less per hectare than men—a gender gap that was costing the country more than $1 billion annually. So, the agriculture ministry, with support from the Gates Foundation, partnered with CARE, an international NGO, on a program that cuts out middlemen by connecting women’s producer groups directly to markets and provides training in climate-conscious farming and nutrition.

Over the past decade, this “Farmer Field and Business School” model has expanded across multiple African countries, yielding strong results. In Burundi, for example, women’s crop yields increased substantially. By pooling savings, sharing market intelligence, and lending to one another, women have been able to diversify their small farming businesses, establish credit histories, and build their confidence.

India offers a parallel example. PANI, a local organization rooted in Gandhian values, has spread climate-conscious farming knowledge and market access from woman to woman across tens of thousands of households through trained community advisers.

Underlying these and other programs is a focus on educating and upskilling women, while addressing the deep-seated gender norms that stifle their opportunities. The Ethiopian project engages men in community dialogues to challenge the norms that treat farming as a male pursuit and household chores as a female domain. The women taking part report greater confidence and decision-making power; both women and men say their partnerships are now stronger as a result.

Philanthropy can play its part by helping to scale proven approaches, by backing emerging innovations that are designed around women’s needs—from climate-resilient crops and livestock to AI-powered digital tools—and by linking international financing to clear gender-equality goals.

One promising example, a climate-finance model led by the International Fund for Agricultural Development, ties funding to measurable gains in women’s economic opportunities—making gender equality part of the investment itself, rather than a secondary objective. The model has already helped direct $118.5 million in investments in several countries, helping rural women gain greater control over land and productive assets, strengthen their livelihoods, and build resilience to climate change.

This last point is crucial, because it is now well established that climate change is hitting women farmers hardest, compounding deep-rooted inequalities. Research in low- and middle-income countries has found that a 1° Celsius rise in average temperatures is associated with a 34% greater reduction in income for female-headed households compared to male-headed households.

As the effects of climate change intensify, governments, development partners, and philanthropic organizations must do more to create conditions for rural women to adapt, build resilience, and prosper. Women like Okonkwo show what is possible. They are already sustaining food systems; positioning them to lead will drive the structural changes our societies need.

Ana Maria Loboguerrero is Director of Adaptive and Equitable Food Systems at the Gates Foundation.

item.title: Low Expectations for Israel’s Election
item.dc:creator: Shlomo Ben-Ami
item.description: Benjamin Netanyahu has led Israel into a trap in which ever-increasing strategic commitments are outstripping the productive base that finances them, and the goodwill on which its alliances depend is being destroyed. While a new government would not transform Israeli foreign policy, it could begin to drag Israel out of its morass.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images

Benjamin Netanyahu has led Israel into a trap in which ever-increasing strategic commitments are outstripping the productive base that finances them, and the goodwill on which its alliances depend is being destroyed. While a new government would not transform Israeli foreign policy, it could begin to drag Israel out of its morass.

By Shlomo Ben-Ami

TEL AVIV—In Hungary’s general election in April, Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s right-wing populist government was toppled not by some leftist opposition, but rather by a center-right party committed to fighting corruption and restoring democracy. As Israel heads to the polls on October 27, a similar shift is by far the best outcome one can reasonably hope for, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s extremist government replaced by a decent, law-abiding administration. A radically new foreign policy will remain out of reach.

item.title: From AI Boom to Economic Bust
item.dc:creator: Ian Goldin
item.description: Contrary to tech optimists' rosy predictions, AI may prove to be a drag on growth. By concentrating wealth and economic opportunities in a few cities while destroying the low-cost jobs that have historically fueled global development, the technology could end up making much of the world poorer and more divided.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Wang Jiang/VCG via Getty Images

Contrary to tech optimists' rosy predictions, AI may prove to be a drag on growth. By concentrating wealth and economic opportunities in a few cities while destroying the low-cost jobs that have historically fueled global development, the technology could end up making much of the world poorer and more divided.

By Ian Goldin

OXFORD—The divide between AI fantasists and doomers is growing. The fantasists believe AI will turbocharge growth and create a utopian world of abundance. The doomers believe it poses an existential threat to humanity and that, before killing us, it will lead to mass unemployment and a world of pervasive surveillance and alternative realities. Who is right? And can governments do anything to mitigate the risk of catastrophe?

LONDON—Two recent conversations confirmed my suspicion that too many experts are operating in silos and often failing to connect the dots.

item.title: Is Christian Democracy Finished?
item.dc:creator: Jan-Werner Mueller
item.description: Traditionally, Christian Democrats believed that taking care of all groups in society could create a harmonious balance that would prevent instability and self-destructive infighting. But the conditions that enabled this strategy have changed, particularly in Germany, where Christian Democrats must reconnect with a different part of their history.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Thomas Nieder/Getty Images

Traditionally, Christian Democrats believed that taking care of all groups in society could create a harmonious balance that would prevent instability and self-destructive infighting. But the conditions that enabled this strategy have changed, particularly in Germany, where Christian Democrats must reconnect with a different part of their history.

By Jan-Werner Mueller

BERLIN—Recent state elections in Germany have been portrayed as momentous, since the far right finished first in two and may well come to power in one. Yet future historians may focus on another, largely overlooked outcome: For the first time in the post-World War II period, Germany’s Christian Democrats (CDU) failed to pass the 5% electoral threshold. Worse, this disastrous result occurred in the largely rural state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, where former Chancellor Angela Merkel chaired the CDU’s state branch for close to seven years.

item.title: Independent AI Auditing Now
item.dc:creator: Angela Huyue Zhang and Yue Zhao
item.description: Recent hacking incidents confirm the need for independent scrutiny not only of what AI systems are capable of, but also of what their developers are doing to minimize harm and communicate honestly with the public. Even if AI auditing is still at an early stage, other industries have already provided a playbook.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: cagkansayin/Getty Images

Recent hacking incidents confirm the need for independent scrutiny not only of what AI systems are capable of, but also of what their developers are doing to minimize harm and communicate honestly with the public. Even if AI auditing is still at an early stage, other industries have already provided a playbook.

By Angela Huyue Zhang and Yue Zhao

LOS ANGELES—Hardly a week goes by without another report of an AI agent from a leading US lab digitally breaching businesses or even government services. In July, OpenAI agents escaped an internal testing environment and attacked the collaboration-platform company Hugging Face. In June, another OpenAI model gained nonpublic access to an Australian government Medicare statistics service while trying to complete a research task. And in the latest revelation, an Anthropic agent broke into the US State Department website and filled out visa applications.

item.title: Strict Liability for AI Executives
item.dc:creator: Danielle Keats Citron
item.description: As an OpenAI whistleblower recently explained, AI executives have knowingly fostered a culture that “guarantees periodic failures,” the scale of which is “growing as systems get more capable.” This approach hinges on an expectation of impunity, which is why AI firms must be held legally accountable for the harm their agents cause.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

As an OpenAI whistleblower recently explained, AI executives have knowingly fostered a culture that “guarantees periodic failures,” the scale of which is “growing as systems get more capable.” This approach hinges on an expectation of impunity, which is why AI firms must be held legally accountable for the harm their agents cause.

By Danielle Keats Citron

CHARLOTTESVILLE—Twenty years ago, I argued that the creation of databases of sensitive information—including home addresses, biometric data, and Social Security numbers—should be understood as ultrahazardous activities. They could be managed only if the entities creating them were held fully liable for breaches. As AI models generate new and extreme risks, the need for a strict-liability regime is urgent. If frontier companies bore strict responsibility for the destruction caused by their AI chatbots and agents, they might slow down to figure out how to conduct their activities safely and change course where that is not possible.

item.title: Who Will Pay to Preserve Tropical Forests?
item.dc:creator: Carlos Nobre and Lee White
item.description: For decades, the international community has acknowledged the extraordinary value of tropical forests while failing to invest adequately in their conservation. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility, launched at last year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference, could help close this financing gap.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Evaristo Sa/AFP via Getty Images

For decades, the international community has acknowledged the extraordinary value of tropical forests while failing to invest adequately in their conservation. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility, launched at last year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference, could help close this financing gap.

By Carlos Nobre and Lee White

SÃO PAULO/STIRLING—The enormous climate, water, and biodiversity benefits generated by tropical forests accrue to the entire world. But hardly any of the economic value created is captured by the countries and communities that safeguard them. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) was launched at last year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30) in Belém to start correcting this imbalance.

For too long, it has been more profitable to destroy tropical forests than to conserve them, even though they provide services essential for the survival of many countries and for the welfare of us all. The Amazon recycles nearly half of its rainfall and exports moisture that shapes precipitation patterns across South America and beyond. The Congo Basin, with its peatlands that store roughly 30 billion tons of carbon, is one of the planet’s great carbon reservoirs, while many of the plant and animal species in Borneo are found nowhere else on Earth.

Moreover, across the tropics, forests support the livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people—including Indigenous communities whose stewardship is often essential for maintaining them—while also sustaining local cultures and bolstering food and water security.

But market prices do not adequately reflect these benefits, creating an economic barrier that all tropical regions bump up against: in the short term, clearing a hectare of forest can generate more income than protecting it, even when the long-term costs of forest loss are much greater. As a result, cattle ranching and agricultural expansion exert enormous pressure on the Amazon, small- and large-scale agriculture contribute to forest conversion in the Congo Basin, and industrial plantations have transformed sylvan landscapes in Southeast Asia.

Worryingly, a recent brief by the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network emphasizes that international public finance remains far below the estimated investment required for conserving tropical forests, and that competition for declining official development aid is intensifying.

Grants and concessional loans remain indispensable for strengthening institutions, protecting rights, restoring degraded landscapes, and supporting activities with large social and ecological returns but limited commercial returns. Yet, traditional development finance alone cannot close the gap. Nor should scarce public resources be used simply to absorb risks for private investors.

This is where the TFFF comes in. It is designed to provide eligible tropical-forest countries with predictable, long-term payments for maintaining forest cover and meeting agreed performance criteria. This changes the economic incentives: according to the TFFF’s current model, countries will forgo around $400 per deforested hectare. Because each hectare of standing tropical forest increases a country’s payment, policymakers may be more willing to implement robust national strategies that complement the TFFF, like Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation (REDD+).

The TFFF’s proposed architecture includes a commitment to direct at least 20% of payments to Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities, who play an outsize role in protecting forests but have historically received only a small share of international climate and nature finance. The real test will be whether this commitment results in predictable funding that reaches those managing forests on the ground and, in the process, reinforces local governance.

Of course, the TFFF is not a silver bullet. No single solution can close the financing gap for tropical-forest conservation. Public and private funding, domestic expenditure, concessional loans, grants, results-based payments, and new investment mechanisms must all play a role. Perhaps more importantly, no financial mechanism can compensate indefinitely for incentives that continue to encourage deforestation. To change them, policymakers must intervene.

The TFFF has a role to play here, too. To succeed, it must not only mobilize enough capital to translate global commitments into predictable payments on the ground, but also support governments in implementing policies that protect forests and complement existing forest-finance instruments. These include strengthening land rights and environmental governance, repurposing harmful subsidies, supporting restoration, and expanding viable economic opportunities compatible with standing forests.

For decades, the international community has acknowledged the extraordinary value of tropical forests while failing to invest adequately in their conservation. Ensuring that they remain standing is in everyone’s interests. The challenge now is to use all tools at our disposal, not least the TFFF, to turn talk into action.

Carlos Nobre, a senior scientist at the University of São Paulo’s Institute of Advanced Studies, is Co-Chair of the Science Panel for the Amazon.

Lee White, a former minister of water, forests, the sea, and environment of Gabon, is an honorary professor at the University of Stirling and Special Envoy of the Science Panel for the Congo Basin.

item.title: Why Following in Milei’s Footsteps Would Be Bad for Brazil
item.dc:creator: Laura Carvalho, Martín Guzmán and Joseph E. Stiglitz
item.description: Far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro holds up Argentine President Javier Milei’s economic program as a model for Brazil. But Milei's economic experiment has been a failure, leaving millions of Argentinians worse off and effectively turning their heavily indebted country into a client of the United States.

item.title: How Worried Should We Be About the Global Economy?
item.dc:creator: Dambisa Moyo
item.description: The risks to the global economy—including high inflation, soaring public debt, market concentration, and geopolitical volatility—are well known. But it is worth underscoring just how rare and dangerous it is for all of them to be salient at the same time.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

The risks to the global economy—including high inflation, soaring public debt, market concentration, and geopolitical volatility—are well known. But it is worth underscoring just how rare and dangerous it is for all of them to be salient at the same time.

By Dambisa Moyo

JAIPUR—It is difficult to remember a time when economies, financial markets, politics, and societies were subject to significant volatility and uncertainty simultaneously, let alone to the degree they are today.

item.title: How a Pause on Frontier AI Could Work
item.dc:creator: Barry Eichengreen, Will Fithian and Wesley Holliday
item.description: Whether the development of frontier AI should be paused is for policymakers to decide. But they should recognize that highly concentrated hardware supply chains make a pause feasible and, if implemented properly, likely to be sustainable.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Sean Gallup/Getty Images

Whether the development of frontier AI should be paused is for policymakers to decide. But they should recognize that highly concentrated hardware supply chains make a pause feasible and, if implemented properly, likely to be sustainable.

By Barry Eichengreen, Will Fithian and Wesley Holliday

BERKELEY—Dario Amodei, a co-founder of Anthropic, among others, has warned that AI poses an existential threat to humankind. Others have gone further and argued for pausing the training of new frontier AI models. The counterargument is that regulation, including self-regulation, is unlikely to be effective. And even if a pause is feasible in principle, there is little hope that it could be sustained in practice, given that the United States and China desperately fear falling behind each other.

item.title: Trump’s Latest Gift to Putin
item.dc:creator: Timothy Snyder
item.description: Unable to win his foolish war against Iran, Donald Trump blames its consequences on Ukraine and uses the lie to justify ending sanctions against Russia, thereby extending that war as well. His diesel deal with the Kremlin is less about lowering gas prices for Americans and more about submitting to Vladimir Putin.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Contributor/Getty Images

Unable to win his foolish war against Iran, Donald Trump blames its consequences on Ukraine and uses the lie to justify ending sanctions against Russia, thereby extending that war as well. His diesel deal with the Kremlin is less about lowering gas prices for Americans and more about submitting to Vladimir Putin.

By Timothy Snyder

TORONTO—Earlier this year, when I first described the guiding principle of Donald Trump’s foreign policy as superpower suicide, it was already obvious that the US President’s war of whimsy against Iran was a strategic catastrophe. Five months on, this failure is all the more glaring. Worse, it has provided Trump with another pretext to reward Russia. Weakness has begotten more weakness.

item.title: China’s Panda Diplomacy Is Losing Its Charm
item.dc:creator: Brahma Chellaney
item.description: Since giving a pair of giant pandas to the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s visit to Beijing, China has used panda loans as a means of projecting a harmless and friendly image globally. But it was always an act—and foreign audiences are no longer falling for it.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty Images

Since giving a pair of giant pandas to the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s visit to Beijing, China has used panda loans as a means of projecting a harmless and friendly image globally. But it was always an act—and foreign audiences are no longer falling for it.

By Brahma Chellaney

BERLIN—During his recent visit to Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping announced that China would send a breeding pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta. The “envoys of friendship,” Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, arrived just a few days later. This is hardly the first time China has used its iconic bear as an instrument of soft power. By loaning the animals to overseas zoos, it seeks to project an image of China not as a threatening dragon, but rather as a tough but cuddly charmer.

item.title: The Blindness of China’s All-Seeing State
item.dc:creator: Yaqiu Wang
item.description: China's relentless surveillance has taught people to perform obedience and loyalty, while keeping their beliefs hidden. This creates a dilemma for the ruling Communist Party: repression distorts the very information the government needs to understand society.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: HouYu/China News Service via Getty Images

China's relentless surveillance has taught people to perform obedience and loyalty, while keeping their beliefs hidden. This creates a dilemma for the ruling Communist Party: repression distorts the very information the government needs to understand society.

By Yaqiu Wang

WASHINGTON, DC—China’s surveillance state reaches into the most banal corners of life. At a garden in Yangzhou, visitors must scan their faces to receive toilet paper; the dispenser remembers them and refuses to provide a second serving. In Shenzhen, the police use facial-recognition technology to catch jaywalkers, then send penalties to scofflaws’ phones and notify their employers. The scrutiny is not limited to public spaces. For China-registered users, WeChat messages and images are automatically screened. One human-rights lawyer recalled that police monitored his WeChat exchanges before detaining and torturing him.

Continues on Project Syndicate (subscriber article)

item.title: A Stronger Renminbi Is No Quick Fix for Global Imbalances
item.dc:creator: Kai Guo
item.description: The near-consensus among financial commentators is that China's currency is undervalued, driving global imbalances. But the renminbi's weakness reflects weak domestic demand, and pursuing currency appreciation without addressing that issue head-on would be counterproductive for everyone.
item.content:encoded:
Photo: CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images

The near-consensus among financial commentators is that China's currency is undervalued, driving global imbalances. But the renminbi's weakness reflects weak domestic demand, and pursuing currency appreciation without addressing that issue head-on would be counterproductive for everyone.

By Kai Guo

BEIJING—The renminbi is back at the center of debates about global macroeconomic imbalances. With China’s merchandise trade surplus widening to $1.2 trillion in 2025, and with its manufacturing sector becoming increasingly dominant, the near-consensus among financial and economic commentators is that the renminbi is significantly undervalued. The implication is that China should let its currency appreciate sharply, thereby shrinking its surplus, easing competitive pressure on manufacturers elsewhere, and helping rebalance the global economy.
